title: What Is a Ductless HVAC System?
h1: What Is a Ductless HVAC System, and Is a Mini Split Right for You?
description: A ductless mini split heats and cools rooms without ductwork, using an outdoor unit and wall-mounted indoor heads. Learn how it works and where it fits best.
quick_answer: A ductless HVAC system, usually called a mini split, heats and cools without ductwork. An outdoor heat pump connects through a small hole in the wall to one or more indoor units mounted in the rooms. Each indoor unit has its own controls, which makes mini splits a good fit for additions, garage conversions, ADUs and homes without ducts.
body:
Many older homes in San Diego and Orange County were built with a wall furnace and no central air, and many newer additions and ADUs were never tied into the main system. Ductless mini splits solve both problems. They're also a common answer for one stubborn room that the central system never keeps comfortable.

How does a ductless mini split work?

A mini split is a heat pump split into two parts:

  • Outdoor unit. It holds the compressor and outdoor coil. It's usually smaller and quieter than a central AC condenser.
  • Indoor units. Often called heads, these hold a coil, a fan and a filter. They blow conditioned air directly into the room.
  • Line set. Refrigerant lines, a power cable and a condensate drain run through a small hole in the wall to connect the two.

Because it's a heat pump, the same system cools in summer and heats in winter. Most mini splits use inverter compressors that speed up and slow down to match the room's needs.

What types of indoor units are there?

  • Wall-mounted heads are the most common and least expensive.
  • Ceiling cassettes sit flush in the ceiling and blow air in several directions.
  • Floor consoles sit low on a wall, useful under windows or in rooms with sloped ceilings.
  • Slim ducted units hide in a ceiling or closet and serve one or two rooms through short ducts.

What is the difference between single-zone and multi-zone?

A single-zone system has one outdoor unit and one indoor head. A multi-zone system connects several indoor heads to one outdoor unit, so you can condition multiple rooms with separate temperature settings. Multi-zone setups save wall space outside but put all rooms on one outdoor unit, so if it fails, every room is affected.

Where do mini splits make the most sense?

  1. Garage conversions, ADUs and room additions
  2. Older homes with no ductwork
  3. Upstairs bedrooms or bonus rooms over a garage that stay hot
  4. Home offices you want comfortable without conditioning the whole house
  5. Homes replacing old wall furnaces or window AC units

What are the pros and cons?

ProsCons
No duct losses in a hot atticIndoor heads are visible on the wall
Room-by-room temperature controlEach head has filters that need regular cleaning
Quiet indoor and outdoor operationWhole-house coverage can take several heads
Heating and cooling in one systemIndoor coils can grow mold if not maintained
Minimal construction to installFiltration is basic compared to a central system

How do you maintain a ductless system?

Mini splits are simple to live with, but they do need care:

  • Rinse the washable filters in each head about once a month, more often with pets or during smoke events.
  • Keep the outdoor unit clear of plants and debris.
  • Watch for water dripping from a head, which usually means a clogged drain.
  • Have the indoor coils and blower wheels professionally cleaned when they get dirty. Musty odors and black specks from the vents are signs it's time.

Near the coast, salt air can affect outdoor coils over time, so yearly checkups are a good idea. Learn more about mini splits and central AC on our air conditioning services page.

What happens during a mini split installation?

Most installs are much less disruptive than adding ductwork. A typical job looks like this:

  1. Choose the best wall or ceiling spot for each indoor head, away from direct sun and with a clear path for air.
  2. Drill a small hole through the wall for the line set and drain.
  3. Set the outdoor unit on a pad or wall bracket.
  4. Run and connect refrigerant lines, wiring and the drain.
  5. Pull a vacuum on the lines, release the refrigerant and test heating and cooling.

A new circuit from the electrical panel is often needed, and a permit is usually required.

Is a mini split better than central air?

It depends on the house. If you have good ductwork and want to condition the whole home evenly, central air or a ducted heat pump is usually simpler. If you have no ducts, poor ducts in a few areas, or rooms that need separate control, a mini split often makes more sense. Some homes use both. A technician can look at your layout and suggest what fits with a free estimate.
faqs: Can a mini split heat a home in winter?
Yes. Mini splits are heat pumps and heat well in our climate, including cold inland nights. They're a common replacement for wall furnaces and electric baseboard heat.
How big of a hole does a mini split need?
Usually a hole about three inches across is enough for the refrigerant lines, power cable and drain. The lines are often covered with a line-hide cover on the outside wall.
Can one outdoor unit run several rooms?
Yes. A multi-zone system connects several indoor heads to one outdoor unit. The number of heads depends on the outdoor unit's capacity and the model.
Why is my mini split dripping water inside?
Dripping usually means the condensate drain is clogged, kinked or not sloped properly, or the coil is dirty. Turn the unit off and have the drain cleared.
